stem: An analyst at Larkspur Outfitters needs to show how monthly revenue changed over the past two years. Which visual is most appropriate?
explanation: A line chart shows change across a continuous time axis, which makes trends easy to read. A pie chart shows parts of a whole at one point in time, a treemap shows hierarchical proportions, and a word cloud shows term frequency in text.

stem: A finance manager wants to show how this year's budget is split across four departments. Which chart type best shows each department's share of the whole?
explanation: With only a few categories at a single point in time, a pie chart clearly shows each part's share of the total. A histogram shows a distribution of one numeric variable, a line chart shows change over time, and a scatter plot shows the relationship between two numeric variables.

stem: Quarry Lane Markets wants to see whether local advertising spend is related to sales across its 220 stores. Which visual should the analyst use?
explanation: A scatter plot places each store at its spend and sales values, so a relationship or correlation becomes visible. A stacked bar shows composition, a donut shows share of a whole, and a gauge shows one value against a target.

stem: A membership director at Brightwater Gyms wants to see how member ages are spread, including where most members cluster. Which chart fits best?
explanation: A histogram groups a numeric variable into bins and shows how often values fall in each, revealing the shape of the distribution. A pie chart shows shares of a whole, a line chart shows a trend over time, and a bubble chart compares three variables per point.

stem: A regional sales leader wants to spot which states have high or low sales at a glance. Which visual best shows this pattern?
explanation: A filled (choropleth) map shades each state by its value, so geographic patterns stand out immediately. A waterfall shows contributions to a running total, a pie with fifty slices is unreadable, and a gauge shows only one overall number.

stem: A controller wants to show how last year's operating profit moved to this year's figure through price, volume and cost changes. Which chart is designed for this?
explanation: A waterfall chart starts at an opening value and shows each positive or negative contribution stepping to the closing value. A stacked area shows composition over time, a radar compares several measures on spokes, and a histogram shows a distribution.

stem: An analyst needs a view that summarizes thousands of order rows into totals by region and quarter, and that users can rearrange by dragging fields. What should they use?
explanation: A pivot table aggregates detail rows into grouped totals and lets users move fields between rows and columns. An infographic is a static designed summary, a scatter plot relates two measures, and a word cloud shows text frequency.

stem: Ashgrove City Library wants a one-page visual for the public that tells the story of last year's programs with icons, a few key numbers and short text. Which format fits best?
explanation: An infographic combines icons, headline figures and brief text into an easy-to-read story for a general audience. A dashboard with slicers and a pivot table assume users who explore data, and a raw export is unreadable for the public.

stem: A line chart shows four product lines in different colors, but readers cannot tell which line is which. Which element should be added?
explanation: A legend maps each color or symbol to the series it represents. Gridlines help read values, a trendline summarizes direction, and a watermark marks status or ownership; none of them identify the series.

stem: Executives reviewing a bar chart of quarterly revenue keep asking for the exact amount of each bar. What is the simplest change?

options.text: Add data labels to the bars

explanation: Data labels print each bar's value directly on or near it, answering the request without extra reading. A second legend does not show values, 3D effects make values harder to read, and removing gridlines removes a reading aid.

stem: Kestrel Advisory is sending a quarterly report to its clients and wants it to be recognized as the firm's work. Which design choice addresses this?

options.text: Use each chart tool's default theme settings
Let each author choose their own colors
Apply the firm's logo, fonts and palette
Add a different clip-art image per page

explanation: Branding means applying the organization's logo, typography and approved colors consistently so the report is identifiable. Default themes and author-chosen colors look generic and inconsistent, and assorted clip art adds clutter rather than identity.

stem: An analyst is shading a table of store results by variance to budget, where values range from large losses through zero to large gains. Which color scheme fits best?

options.text: Qualitative scheme of several unrelated hues
Diverging scheme with a neutral midpoint

explanation: A diverging scheme uses two contrasting hues that meet at a neutral color for zero, so readers see direction and size of variance. A sequential scheme suits values running low to high, a qualitative scheme suits unordered categories, and a rainbow scheme implies false steps and is hard to read.

stem: A map will shade counties by the number of registered voters, from few to many. Which color scheme should the analyst choose?

options.text: Sequential, light to dark in one hue
Diverging, two hues around a midpoint
Qualitative, a distinct hue per county
Alternating, two hues in a checkerboard

explanation: Counts that run from low to high with no meaningful midpoint suit a sequential scheme, where darker means more. A diverging scheme implies a central reference value, a qualitative scheme suggests unordered categories, and alternating hues hide the magnitude.

stem: A status dashboard marks projects on track in green and at risk in red. Several users have red-green color-vision deficiency. What is the best fix?

options.text: Make the green and the red brighter
Add icons or text labels to each status
Swap the green and red meanings
Use darker and lighter shades of red

explanation: Pairing color with a second cue, such as an icon or label, means status is readable without relying on color perception. Brighter or swapped red and green remain hard to tell apart, and two shades of red are easily confused.

stem: An analyst must compare total sales across 14 product categories, many of which have long names. Which visual will be easiest to read?
explanation: Horizontal bars give long category names room and, when sorted, make ranking obvious. A 14-slice pie is hard to compare, a line implies an ordered sequence the categories do not have, and a 14-spoke radar is cluttered.

stem: Marketing wants to show how each of five channels' share of total leads changed across eight quarters. Which visual best fits?

options.text: A single pie chart for one quarter

explanation: A 100% stacked column chart shows each quarter as a whole and each channel's share within it, so shifts in mix over time are visible. A single pie shows only one period, a scatter plot relates two measures, and a histogram shows a distribution.

stem: A merchandiser wants one visual showing sales by department and, nested inside each, by product category, sized by contribution to the total. Which chart fits?
explanation: A treemap draws nested rectangles sized by value, so it shows hierarchy and part-to-whole at once. A line chart shows trends, a histogram shows a distribution, and a gauge shows one value against a target.

stem: A dashboard needs to show this month's customer satisfaction score as one prominent number with its change from last month. Which element fits best?
explanation: A KPI card displays a single headline value, often with a change indicator, so it can be read in a glance. A scatter plot and heat map show many data points, and a pivot table shows grouped totals in rows and columns.

stem: A call center manager wants to see which hour of which weekday gets the most calls, using a grid of days by hours. Which visual fits?
explanation: A heat map shades each cell of a two-way grid by value, so busy day-and-hour combinations stand out. A waterfall shows contributions to a total, a donut shows shares of a whole, and a bubble map places values on geography.

stem: A bar chart's vertical axis starts at 950, making a store with 980 sales look three times larger than one with 960. What should the analyst change?

options.text: Add a trendline across the bars
Use a darker color for the larger bar
Start the value axis at zero

explanation: Bar length encodes value, so a bar chart's axis should start at zero to keep proportions honest. A trendline, 3D effect or darker color does not fix the distorted lengths and can add further distortion.
searchTerm: bar chart axis starting at zero

stem: A draft pie chart has 15 slices, many under 2%, and readers cannot compare them. What is the best alternative?

options.text: A bar chart sorted by value
A 3D version of the pie chart
A pie chart with brighter colors

explanation: Bars on a common baseline let readers compare many small values precisely, and sorting shows rank. 3D pies distort slice sizes, a donut with many rings is no easier to read, and brighter colors do not fix the comparison problem.

stem: A chart is titled "Chart 3" in a monthly report. Which title would best help readers understand it without other context?

options.text: Online Sales by Month, Jan to Jun 2026

explanation: A good title states the measure, the breakdown and the time period so the chart stands on its own. The other titles are generic and do not say what is measured or for when.

stem: A reviewer cannot tell whether a chart's vertical axis shows dollars, units or percentages. Which design element is missing?
explanation: An axis title states what the axis measures and in which units. A legend identifies series, a source note says where data came from, and a logo is branding; none define the axis.

stem: An analyst must show monthly revenue in millions of dollars together with gross margin as a percentage on one visual. Which approach works best?

options.text: Stacked column of both measures together
Two lines on one shared axis
Combo chart with a secondary axis

explanation: A combo chart, such as columns for revenue and a line for margin on a secondary axis, shows two measures with different scales together. Monthly pies cannot show a trend, stacking adds unlike units, and a shared axis flattens the percentage line near zero.

stem: An analyst wants to plot countries by income and life expectancy while also showing each country's population. Which chart type supports all three measures?
explanation: A bubble chart uses horizontal position, vertical position and bubble size for three measures. A pie shows one measure's shares, a histogram shows one variable's distribution, and a waterfall shows contributions to a total.

stem: A filled map of total insurance claims by state shows the most populous states darkest, hiding where claim rates are really high. What should the analyst do?

options.text: Replace the map with a pie chart

explanation: Normalizing by population turns raw counts into rates, so shading reflects risk rather than state size. A rainbow scheme does not fix the measure, removing the legend hides the scale, and a pie loses the geography.

stem: A buyer wants to see sales subtotals by category and then expand any category to see its individual products. Which feature of a pivot table supports this?
explanation: Placing category above product in the rows creates a hierarchy with subtotals that can be expanded or collapsed. Conditional formatting colors cells, a calculated field adds a measure, and a report filter limits the data shown.

stem: Analysts at Orchard Point Bank build dozens of reports, and each uses different fonts and colors. What is the most efficient way to apply consistent branding?

options.text: Review each chart's colors by hand one by one
Ask readers to ignore the differences
Add the logo only to the cover page
Build a shared report theme or template

explanation: A shared theme or template applies approved fonts, colors and logo placement to every report automatically. Manual review is slow and error-prone, ignoring differences weakens the brand, and a cover logo alone leaves the rest inconsistent.

stem: A line chart shows four colored series with no context, and readers do not know what is plotted or in what units. Which TWO additions help most?
explanation: A legend tells readers which series each color represents, and axis titles state what is measured and in which units. 3D effects distort values, extra gridlines add clutter, and a background image distracts without adding meaning.

stem: Which TWO chart types are well suited to showing how a value changes over a continuous time period?
explanation: Line and area charts plot values along a time axis, making trends easy to follow. Pie and donut charts show shares of a whole at one moment, and a treemap shows hierarchical proportions rather than change over time.

stem: Tallowbrook County is redesigning a public dashboard to meet accessibility guidelines. Which THREE color practices should the designer follow?

options.text: Pair red and green for good and bad
Keep strong contrast with the background
Use a dozen bright hues for variety
Place light gray text on white
Add labels so color is not the only cue

explanation: Sufficient contrast, a colorblind-safe palette and a non-color cue such as a label make charts readable for more users. Red-green pairs fail common color-vision deficiencies, many bright hues overwhelm readers, and light gray on white lacks contrast.

stem: An analyst is deciding whether a map is the right visual for store performance. Which TWO conditions make a map appropriate?

options.text: Readers need exact values ranked in order
The data has fields such as state or postal code
All stores are in one building
The data has no location attributes
Location patterns matter to the question asked

explanation: A map needs geographic fields and is worth using when where something happens matters. Exact ranked values are clearer in a sorted bar chart, a single building gives no geographic spread, and data without location cannot be mapped.

stem: Which TWO tasks is a pivot table designed to perform?

options.text: Sum or average values by group
Swap fields between rows and columns
Apply a corporate theme to a report

explanation: A pivot table aggregates values by grouping fields and lets users pivot fields between rows and columns to change the view. Geocoding is a mapping task, key enforcement is a database function, and theming is a branding feature.

stem: Which TWO elements are part of an organization's visual branding in a report?
explanation: Logos and approved colors identify the organization and are core branding elements. Data labels, trendlines and gridlines are chart elements that help read data rather than express identity.

stem: For which TWO situations is an infographic a good fit?

options.text: An annual impact summary for donors
Ad hoc exploration of sales by product
A poster explaining a recycling process
A line-by-line audit of expense claims

explanation: Infographics tell a fixed story with icons, headline numbers and short text for a broad audience, such as donors or the public. Live monitoring needs a refreshing dashboard, exploration needs interactive tools, and an audit needs detailed records.

stem: A chart will be copied into several slide decks and must make sense on its own. Which THREE elements should it include?
explanation: A title, axis titles with units and a legend give readers what, how much and which series without other context. A 3D frame, clip art and a gradient background are decoration that adds clutter without meaning.

stem: A reviewer is checking a draft report for visuals that could mislead readers. Which TWO should be flagged?

options.text: A bar chart sorted from largest to smallest
A tilted 3D pie that enlarges front slices
A line chart with labeled axes and units
A bar chart whose axis starts at 90%
The same color for a region on every page

explanation: Tilted 3D pies make front slices look larger, and a truncated bar axis exaggerates small differences. Sorting bars, labeling axes with units and keeping category colors consistent all make visuals easier to read correctly.

stem: A dashboard has four tiles, each answering one question. Drop the best visual type onto each tile.

nodes.text: Totals by product and region that the viewer rearranges

explanation: A line chart shows change over time, a filled map shows values by place, a pie chart shows parts of a whole for a few categories, and a pivot table lets viewers regroup totals. A scatter plot compares two numeric measures and fits none of the four tiles.

partExplanations.z1: Trends over time are best shown by a line.
partExplanations.z2: Values by state are geographic, so a filled map fits.
partExplanations.z3: A few categories making up one whole suit a pie chart.
partExplanations.z4: A pivot table lets the viewer regroup and total the data.

stem: Label the parts of this sales report page with the design element each one is.

nodes.text: Key explaining that blue is online and orange is stores
Company logo and brand font in the header
Exact values printed above each bar

explanation: A legend explains what each series color means, branding ties the page to the company identity, and data labels print exact values on the marks. An axis title names the measure along an axis, which no node shows.

partExplanations.z1: The key that maps colors to series is a legend.
partExplanations.z2: A logo and brand font are branding.
partExplanations.z3: Values printed on the bars are data labels.

stem: A board dashboard is being reviewed for readability. Select every element that makes the visual harder to read or misleading.

nodes.text: Status shown only as red or green

spots.name: Status shown only as red or green

explanation: Too many slices in a 3-D pie, a truncated bar axis, and a red/green-only status all hurt accuracy or accessibility. A titled line chart, a nearby legend and a logo are sound practice.

partExplanations.pie3d: Fourteen slices in 3-D are hard to compare.
partExplanations.trunc: Starting the bars at 90 exaggerates differences.
partExplanations.legend: A nearby legend makes the colors easy to decode.
partExplanations.rg: Red and green alone fail viewers with color blindness.

stem: A report must follow the company brand guide. Select every element that the brand guide would control.
explanation: Logo rules, a color palette and a heading font are brand identity. The axis scale, the data values and the calculation logic are analytic decisions that a brand guide does not set.

partExplanations.logo: Logo use is a brand rule.
partExplanations.axis: The axis scale follows the data, not the brand.
partExplanations.palette: An approved palette is a core brand rule.
partExplanations.values: Data values come from the source.
partExplanations.font: Typefaces are set by the brand guide.
partExplanations.calc: Calculation logic is an analytic choice.

stem: A pivot table is built from the unit sales rows below. Answer each question about its totals.

payload.caption: Units sold, one row per order line

fields.label: Pivot total of Units for East
Pivot total of Units for West and Widget

explanation: East is 30 + 20 + 10 = 60. West Widget is 45 + 5 = 50. All units total 125, and Widget units are 30 + 45 + 10 + 5 = 90, so the share is 90 / 125 = 72%.

stem: Match each purpose to the design element that serves it.

prompts.text: Explains what each series color represents
States the unit being measured along an axis
Prints exact numbers on the marks
Keeps a report consistent with the company identity

explanation: Each element has one job: the legend decodes color, the axis title names the unit, data labels give exact values and branding gives identity. A filter changes which data appears and is not a design label.

partExplanations.p2: The axis title names the measure and unit.
